key_findings: Exact binding depends on a trustworthy reference anchor; tuple equality alone is not an authority proof.
Verifier-current reference accepts only exact-current attestation and rejects all substituted variants.

A verifier reference one generation stale accepts the matching stale-generation attestation under naive tuple equality, demonstrating false-positive authority when currentness is not separately enforced.

A sibling-context reference accepts the corresponding context-substituted attestation under naive tuple equality, demonstrating context rollback/substitution when currentness is not separately enforced.
Participant-supplied reference accepts every variant by construction; this is circular validation rather than independent verification.

Cross-authority reference accepts exact-current tuple equality even though the source is outside the local authority domain, showing that subject × attribute × generation × context is insufficient when authority provenance is external to those coordinates.
Accepted invalid/reference-compromised evidence does not always improve allocation; acceptance and exploitability remain separate measurements.
The safe boundary therefore requires reference provenance/currentness before tuple equality can confer authority.
design_implication: Treat the expected binding tuple as a separate verifier-owned witness: source identity, authority namespace, lifecycle generation and current decision context must be validated before attestation equality can produce an authoritative input.
claim_ceiling: Deterministic synthetic reference-provenance/currentness experiment only; no real cryptographic key custody, trusted hardware, empirical attacker behavior, calibrated uncertainty, equilibrium, legal finality, interoperability conformance, or production-readiness claim.
